modules.title: Cash Flow & Budgeting
modules.tagline: Know where your money goes before you tell it where to go.
objectives: Distinguish gross pay, take-home pay, fixed and variable expenses, and discretionary spending
Build a percentage-based budget and compute a personal savings rate
Construct a monthly cash-flow statement and read it for leaks
Set an emergency-fund target using real monthly expenses

lessons.title: The anatomy of a budget
glossary: budget
A forward-looking plan for expected income and expenses over a period, usually a month.
fixed expense
A cost that stays roughly constant each period, such as rent or a loan payment.
variable expense
A cost that changes month to month, such as groceries, fuel, or utilities.
discretionary spending
Optional spending you could reduce or cut without an immediate crisis.
take-home pay
Income remaining after taxes, payroll deductions, and benefit premiums — the money you can actually budget.

blocks.html: A budget is a plan for the money you expect to receive and spend over a period — usually a month. It converts vague intentions (I should save more) into concrete numbers you can check against reality. A budget is not a punishment; it is a decision you make once so you do not have to re-decide every purchase.

blocks.text: Gross pay is not your budget

blocks.html: The number on a job offer is gross pay. What lands in your account is take-home pay — gross minus income tax withholding, payroll taxes (Social Security and Medicare), retirement contributions, and insurance premiums. Budget the money you actually control, not the headline salary.

Most durable budgets split take-home pay into three broad buckets: <mark>needs</mark> (housing, food, transport, minimum debt payments, utilities), <mark>wants</mark> (dining out, subscriptions, hobbies, travel), and <mark>savings</mark> (emergency fund, investing, extra debt payoff).

blocks.label: A starting ratio
blocks.html: The 50/30/20 guideline — 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings — is a useful default, not a law. In high-cost cities needs alone may exceed 50%; the response is to widen the gap elsewhere, not to abandon the framework.

items.label: Rent / mortgage
items.html: Need — housing is non-negotiable, though its size is a choice.

items.label: Streaming subscriptions
items.html: Want — discretionary and easy to pause.

items.label: Minimum loan payment
items.html: Need — skipping it triggers fees and credit damage.

items.label: Roth IRA deposit
items.html: Savings — paying your future self first.

blocks.html: The single most important habit is not the exact percentages — it is tracking. You cannot manage what you never measure, and almost everyone underestimates variable spending until they write it down for one full month.

blocks.q: In the 50/30/20 guideline, which bucket does a streaming subscription fall into?
blocks.explain: A subscription is discretionary — you could cancel it tomorrow without a crisis — so it belongs in 'wants'.

lessons.title: Building a cash-flow statement
glossary: cash-flow statement
A record of money in versus money out over a period; positive cash flow means income exceeds spending.
net cash flow
Total income minus total expenses for the period.
zero-based budget
A method where every dollar of income is assigned a job until income minus assignments equals zero.

blocks.html: A budget is a plan; a cash-flow statement is the scoreboard. It lists every dollar that came in and every dollar that went out over the month, and the difference is your net cash flow. Positive net cash flow is the raw material of wealth — it is the money available to save, invest, or repay debt.

blocks.title: Build it in five steps
steps: Sum all take-home pay and any side income for the month.
Rent, insurance, loan minimums, subscriptions — costs you can predict.
Groceries, fuel, dining, utilities — pull from bank and card statements.
Give every leftover dollar a job: emergency fund, investing, or extra debt payoff.

blocks.html: In this example the household ends the month with $857 unassigned. In a zero-based budget that surplus is not left to drift — it is deliberately routed (say $457 to the Roth IRA and $400 to extra loan payoff) so income minus assignments equals zero.

blocks.label: The leak test
blocks.html: If your statement shows a surplus but your bank balance never grows, the surplus is leaking through untracked cash, buy-now-pay-later, or forgotten subscriptions. Reconcile the plan against your actual ending balance.

A cash-flow statement is a pre-flight checklist. Pilots do not skip it because they feel confident; they run it because small unnoticed problems compound at altitude. Your money is the same — the ten-minute monthly review catches the leak before it drains the tank.

options: Total income minus total expenses for the period
The balance in your checking account
blocks.explain: Net cash flow is simply money in minus money out over the period. A positive figure is what you have available to save, invest, or repay debt.

lessons.title: Savings rate and the emergency fund
glossary: savings rate
The share of take-home (or gross) income you save or invest, expressed as a percentage.
emergency fund
Liquid cash set aside to cover unexpected costs or income loss without borrowing.
liquidity
How quickly an asset can be turned into spendable cash without loss of value.

blocks.html: Your savings rate — the percentage of income you keep — is the single most predictive number in personal finance, more than your salary and more than your investment returns in the early years. Savings rate = amount saved ÷ income.

From the earlier statement, routing $857 of $3,367 take-home gives a savings rate of 857 ÷ 3,367 ≈ 25%. A higher savings rate does two things at once: it builds the pile faster and lowers the pile you need, because you have trained yourself to live on less.

blocks.text: How big should the emergency fund be?

blocks.html: The target is measured in months of essential expenses, not months of income. Add up needs only — housing, food, utilities, transport, minimum debt payments, insurance — and multiply.

head: Situation
Recommended buffer
rows: Single income or some job risk
Variable income, freelance, or sole earner with dependents

blocks.html: If essentials are $2,510/month, a six-month fund is 6 × $2,510 = $15,060. Keep it in a high-yield savings account — high liquidity, insured, and boring on purpose. This money is not an investment; its job is to exist the day you need it.

blocks.label: Order of operations
blocks.html: A common sequence: (1) a $1,000 starter buffer, (2) capture any employer 401(k) match, (3) pay off high-interest debt, (4) build the full 3-6 month fund, (5) invest for long-term goals. The match comes early because it is an instant 50-100% return.

blocks.q: A household with $3,000/month of essential expenses wants a five-month emergency fund. What is the target?
blocks.explain: Five months of essentials = 5 x $3,000 = $15,000. The fund is sized on essential expenses, not gross income.

questions.q: What is the first habit that makes any budget work?
questions.explain: Tracking reveals reality. The percentages are just a target to steer toward once you know your real numbers.

questions.q: Which of these is a fixed expense?
questions.explain: Rent is contractually the same each month, so it is fixed. The others fluctuate and are variable.

questions.q: Which figure should a monthly budget be built on?
questions.explain: Take-home pay is the money you actually receive and control after taxes and deductions — that is what you can assign.

questions.q: A savings rate is calculated as:
questions.explain: Savings rate = amount saved / income. It is the most predictive early-career wealth metric.

questions.q: An emergency fund's size should be based on:
questions.explain: The fund must cover essential expenses during a disruption, so it is measured in months of essentials, not income.

questions.q: What is the common name for liquid cash set aside to cover surprises without borrowing? (two words)
questions.explain: An emergency fund is your first savings priority and is kept liquid and insured, not invested.

questions.q: Which of these typically count as 'needs'?
questions.explain: Concert tickets are discretionary wants. Housing, minimum debt payments, and basic groceries are needs.

questions.q: In a ______-based budget, every dollar of income is assigned a job until the leftover equals zero. (one word)
questions.explain: A zero-based budget assigns every dollar a purpose so nothing drifts unallocated.

modules.title: The Time Value of Money
modules.tagline: A dollar today outranks a dollar tomorrow — and the gap is math you can compute.
objectives: State why money has time value and define present and future value
Apply the compound-interest formula FV = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) to real numbers
Use the future-value-of-an-annuity formula to value regular contributions
Estimate doubling time with the Rule of 72 and reason about inflation

lessons.title: Present value, future value, and compounding
glossary: time value of money
The principle that a sum available now is worth more than the same sum later, because it can earn a return.
present value
What a future sum is worth today, discounted at a given rate.
future value
What a present sum will grow to by a future date at a given rate.
compounding
When investment returns themselves earn further returns over time.
principal
The original amount invested or borrowed, before interest.

blocks.html: The <mark>time value of money</mark> is the idea that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because today's dollar can be put to work and earn a return. Every serious money decision — loans, investing, retirement, even lottery payouts — is an application of this one principle.

Think of a snowball rolling downhill. It does not collect snow at a steady rate — the bigger it gets, the more surface it has to gather even more. Time on the hill matters more than how hard you push at the top. Compound interest is that snowball made of money.
Future value from a single lump sum is:

blocks.code:
FV = P * (1 + r/n)^(n*t)

P = principal (starting amount)
r = annual interest rate (as a decimal)
n = compounding periods per year
t = number of years

blocks.html: Worked example. Invest P = $10,000 at r = 7% (0.07), compounded annually (n = 1), for t = 30 years:

blocks.title: Compute FV of $10,000 at 7% for 30 years

blocks.html: The $10,000 became about $76,123 without adding another cent — roughly 7.6x. Of that gain, the overwhelming majority is interest earning interest, not the original deposit.

blocks.label: The cost of waiting
blocks.html: Because compounding rewards time, starting five years earlier often beats saving twice as much later. The same $10,000 for only 20 years grows to about $38,700 — less than half — even though you waited just a third less time. The most expensive mistake is delay.

blocks.caption: Growth is trivial early, dominant late — time in the market beats a bigger late deposit.

blocks.q: In FV = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), which variable does compounding reward most dramatically because it sits in the exponent?
blocks.explain: Time t appears in the exponent, so small increases in years produce large increases in future value. That is why starting early is so powerful.

lessons.title: Valuing regular contributions and doubling time
glossary: annuity
A series of equal payments made at regular intervals.
future value of an annuity
What a stream of equal periodic contributions grows to by a future date.
Rule of 72
A shortcut: dividing 72 by the annual percent return estimates the years to double.
real return
An investment return after subtracting inflation; it reflects true gain in purchasing power.

blocks.html: Most people do not invest one lump sum — they contribute a fixed amount every month. A stream of equal payments is an <mark>annuity</mark>, and its future value has its own formula:

blocks.code:
FV = PMT * [ ((1 + r)^N - 1) / r ]

PMT = payment per period
r   = rate per period
N   = total number of periods

blocks.html: Worked example. Contribute PMT = $500 per month, at 7% annual (r = 0.07/12 ≈ 0.005833 per month), for 30 years (N = 360 months):
Contributions total $500 × 360 = $180,000, but the account holds roughly $610,000. About $430,000 — more than two-thirds — is growth. Consistency plus time did the heavy lifting.

blocks.html: To estimate how long money takes to double, divide 72 by the annual percent return. At 7%, 72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10.3 years to double. At 9%, about 8 years. This mental shortcut lets you sanity-check any growth claim without a calculator.

blocks.label: Inflation runs the clock backward
blocks.html: If investments return 7% but inflation is 3%, your <mark>real return</mark> is only about 4%. Purchasing power, not the raw balance, is what buys groceries in 30 years. Always reason in real terms for long horizons.

blocks.q: Using the Rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double at a 6% annual return?
blocks.explain: 72 / 6 = 12 years. The Rule of 72 is an estimate but is accurate enough for quick planning at typical rates.

questions.q: The time value of money says that:
options: Money loses value in a safe
A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later
questions.explain: A dollar today can earn a return, so it is worth more than the same dollar received later.

questions.q: In FV = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), what does n represent?
questions.explain: n is how many times per year interest compounds; monthly is 12, quarterly is 4, annually is 1.

questions.q: $10,000 invested at 7% compounded annually for 30 years grows to approximately:
Compounding accelerates over time primarily because:
questions.explain: Growth stacking on prior growth is the engine of compounding, which is why the curve steepens with time.

questions.q: If your investments return 7% and inflation is 3%, your approximate real return is:
questions.explain: Real return is roughly nominal return minus inflation: 7% - 3% = 4% of true purchasing-power gain.

questions.q: The shortcut that divides 72 by the annual percent return to estimate doubling time is called the Rule of ______. (number)
questions.explain: The Rule of 72 estimates years to double; 72 divided by the rate gives the answer.

questions.q: Which factors increase the future value of a lump-sum investment?
questions.explain: Higher rate, more time, and more frequent compounding all increase FV. A lower principal decreases it.

questions.q: Contributing $500/month at 7% for 30 years yields roughly $610,000 on $180,000 contributed. The extra ~$430,000 is:
questions.explain: The gap between contributions and ending balance is compound growth — returns earning further returns.

modules.title: Debt, Credit & Amortization
modules.tagline: The same compounding that builds wealth can bury you when it runs in reverse.
objectives: Interpret APR, interest, and the difference between good and bad debt
Read an amortization schedule and compute a fixed loan payment
Compare minimum payments against aggressive payoff on a credit card
Explain what drives a credit score and how to protect it

lessons.title: APR, interest, and the two kinds of debt
glossary: APR
Annual Percentage Rate — the yearly cost of borrowing, including certain fees, expressed as a percentage.
principal
The outstanding amount borrowed on which interest is charged.
compound interest
Interest charged on both the principal and previously accrued interest.
good debt
Borrowing that funds an appreciating asset or higher future income, ideally at a low rate.
bad debt
High-rate borrowing for depreciating consumption, where interest outruns any benefit.

blocks.html: APR (Annual Percentage Rate) is the yearly price of borrowing money. A 22% APR credit card charges roughly 22 ÷ 12 ≈ 1.83% per month on the balance you carry. Because that interest is added to the balance and then itself charged interest, compound interest works against you exactly as hard as it works for an investor.

items.label: Mortgage (3-7%)
items.html: Often 'good' — funds an asset that may appreciate; interest may be tax-deductible.

items.label: Federal student loan (4-8%)
items.html: Can be good if it raises lifetime income; borrow deliberately.

items.label: Auto loan (5-10%)
items.html: Neutral to bad — the car depreciates while you pay interest.

items.label: Credit card / payday (20-400%)
items.html: Almost always bad — high-rate borrowing for consumption. Attack first.

blocks.html: The distinction between <mark>good debt</mark> and <mark>bad debt</mark> is not moral — it is arithmetic. Debt is defensible when the rate is low and the money buys something that appreciates or raises your income. It is destructive when a high rate compounds against a purchase that is losing value.

blocks.label: The rate hurdle
blocks.html: Paying off a 22% credit card is a guaranteed, tax-free 22% return — better than almost any investment can promise. This is why high-interest debt payoff usually beats investing on a pure-numbers basis.

blocks.q: Why is paying off a 22% APR credit card often described as a guaranteed 22% return?
options: Every dollar of balance eliminated avoids 22% of future interest you would otherwise pay
blocks.explain: Eliminating a 22% balance avoids 22% in future interest with certainty — an outcome no ordinary investment can guarantee.

lessons.title: Amortization: how a fixed payment splits
glossary: amortization
Paying off a loan through equal periodic payments that cover interest first, then reduce principal.
amortization schedule
A table showing, for each payment, how much goes to interest versus principal and the remaining balance.
fixed-rate loan
A loan whose interest rate and payment stay constant for the full term.

blocks.html: A fixed-rate loan is repaid through <mark>amortization</mark>: equal payments, each split between interest (charged on the current balance) and principal (which shrinks the balance). Early payments are mostly interest; later payments are mostly principal. The monthly payment comes from this formula:

blocks.code:
M = P * [ r(1 + r)^N ] / [ (1 + r)^N - 1 ]

M = monthly payment
P = loan principal
r = monthly interest rate (APR / 12)
N = total number of payments

blocks.html: Worked example. A $20,000 auto loan at 6% APR (r = 0.005/month) over 5 years (N = 60):
Total paid = $386.66 × 60 ≈ $23,200, so interest costs about $3,200 on a $20,000 loan. Watch how the first and last payments split:

blocks.label: Why extra principal payments are powerful early
blocks.html: An extra $100 applied to principal in month 1 removes that dollar from every future interest calculation for the rest of the term. The earlier in an amortization schedule you overpay, the more total interest you erase.

blocks.caption: Fixed payments shift gradually from mostly interest to mostly principal.

blocks.q: In an amortization schedule, why is the first payment mostly interest?
options: Interest is charged on the balance, which is largest at the start
The rate is higher early on
blocks.explain: Interest each month is the rate times the current balance. Early on the balance is largest, so the interest portion is largest.

lessons.title: Minimum payments vs aggressive payoff
glossary: minimum payment
The smallest amount a lender requires each month, often ~2% of the balance, designed to maximize interest collected.
debt avalanche
Paying minimums on all debts and throwing extra cash at the highest-APR debt first.
debt snowball
Paying minimums on all debts and clearing the smallest balance first for psychological momentum.

blocks.html: The <mark>minimum payment</mark> on a credit card — often about 2% of the balance — is engineered to keep you in debt as long as legally comfortable. Consider a $5,000 balance at 22% APR (1.833%/month).

blocks.caption: Minimum-only drags on for years; a fixed $200/mo clears it in ~34 months.

blocks.html: Paying a fixed $200/month clears the $5,000 in about 34 months with roughly $1,750 of interest. Paying only the 2% minimum (which shrinks as the balance shrinks) can stretch repayment past a decade and cost more in interest than the original purchase — a textbook case of compounding running against you.

tabs.label: Avalanche
tabs.html: Pay minimums everywhere, then attack the highest-APR debt first. This minimizes total interest paid — it is the mathematically optimal strategy.

tabs.label: Snowball
tabs.html: Pay minimums everywhere, then clear the smallest balance first. It costs slightly more interest but delivers a quick win that keeps many people motivated to continue.

blocks.label: Which to choose
blocks.html: The <mark>debt avalanche</mark> wins on math; the <mark>debt snowball</mark> wins on psychology. The best plan is the one you will actually finish — a completed snowball beats an abandoned avalanche.

blocks.q: The debt avalanche method directs extra payments toward the debt with the:
blocks.explain: The avalanche targets the highest APR first, which minimizes total interest paid across all debts.

lessons.title: Credit scores and how to protect them
glossary: credit score
A number (commonly 300-850) estimating the likelihood you will repay borrowed money on time.
credit utilization
The share of your available revolving credit you are using; lower is better.
hard inquiry
A lender's credit check when you apply for new credit, which can slightly lower your score.
credit report
A detailed record of your credit accounts, payment history, and inquiries maintained by credit bureaus.

blocks.html: A <mark>credit score</mark> (typically 300-850 on the FICO scale) is a lender's estimate of your reliability. It affects loan approvals, interest rates, insurance premiums, apartment applications, and sometimes hiring. A higher score can mean tens of thousands of dollars less in lifetime interest.

head: FICO factor
Approx. weight
What it measures
rows: Whether you pay on time — the single biggest factor
How much of your available credit you are using
Variety of credit types (cards, installment loans)
Recently opened accounts and hard inquiries

blocks.html: The two dominant levers are within your control. Pay every bill on time (35%) and keep credit utilization low (30%). Utilization is your balance divided by your limit — if you have a $10,000 limit and carry $3,000, that is 30% utilization. Aim to keep it under about 30%, and under 10% is even better.

cards.label: Do: automate minimums
cards.html: One missed payment can drop a good score by 50-100 points and linger for years. Autopay the minimum so you are never late by accident.

cards.label: Don't: close old cards
cards.html: Closing an old card shortens your average account age and cuts your total limit, raising utilization. Usually keep old no-fee cards open.

cards.label: Do: check reports free
cards.html: You can pull your reports from the three bureaus at no cost via AnnualCreditReport.com and dispute errors.

cards.label: Don't: chase every offer
cards.html: Each application is a hard inquiry. A cluster of inquiries signals risk and dents your score.

blocks.label: Carrying a balance does NOT help your score
blocks.html: A persistent myth: you do not need to carry credit-card debt to build credit. Using the card and paying it in full every month builds history and avoids all interest. Utilization is measured at the statement date, not by how much interest you pay.

blocks.q: Which two factors carry the most weight in a FICO score?
options: Length of history and credit mix
blocks.explain: Payment history (~35%) and amounts owed/utilization (~30%) together account for about two-thirds of the score.

questions.q: A 22% APR corresponds to roughly what monthly interest rate on a carried balance?
questions.explain: APR divided by 12: 22% / 12 is about 1.83% charged per month on the balance.

questions.q: In an amortizing loan, early payments consist mostly of:
questions.explain: Interest is charged on the balance, which is largest at the start, so early payments are mostly interest.

questions.q: The debt avalanche method minimizes total interest by targeting:
questions.explain: Attacking the highest APR first eliminates the most expensive interest, minimizing the total paid.

questions.q: Credit utilization is defined as:
questions.explain: Utilization is the balance you carry divided by your available limit; lower is better for your score.

questions.q: Which single factor has the largest weight in a FICO score?
questions.explain: Payment history is about 35% of the score — paying on time matters more than anything else.

questions.q: Paying off a fixed-rate loan through equal periodic payments that cover interest then reduce principal is called ______. (one word)
questions.explain: Amortization spreads repayment into equal payments, front-loaded with interest and back-loaded with principal.

questions.q: Which habits generally help a credit score?
options: Applying for many cards at once
questions.explain: On-time payments and low utilization help. Closing old cards and rapid applications hurt.

questions.q: Carrying a credit-card balance month to month:
options: Costs interest with no scoring benefit
questions.explain: You build credit by using the card and paying in full; carrying a balance only adds interest cost.

modules.title: Taxes: The Basics Everyone Needs
modules.tagline: You are taxed on what you keep — knowing the rules changes what you keep.
objectives: Distinguish gross income, adjusted gross income, and taxable income
Explain marginal versus effective tax rates and progressive brackets
Contrast the standard deduction with itemizing and use tax-advantaged accounts
Describe how withholding, credits, and deductions differ

lessons.title: How income tax actually works
glossary: gross income
Total income from all sources before any deductions.
adjusted gross income
Gross income minus specific 'above-the-line' adjustments; AGI drives many phase-outs.
taxable income
AGI minus the standard or itemized deduction; the amount brackets are applied to.
marginal tax rate
The rate applied to your next dollar of income — your top bracket.
effective tax rate
Total tax divided by total income — your true average rate.
progressive tax
A system where higher income is taxed at higher marginal rates, bracket by bracket.

blocks.html: The most common tax misconception is that moving into a higher bracket taxes all your income at that rate. It does not. The U.S. federal income tax is progressive: each bracket's rate applies only to the income within that bracket. This is the difference between your marginal tax rate and your effective tax rate.

blocks.label: Numbers change every year
blocks.html: Bracket thresholds and the standard deduction are indexed to inflation and revised annually. The figures below use 2026 single-filer brackets — always confirm the current year's values with the IRS.
Worked example (single filer, 2026 brackets). Suppose taxable income is $60,000 and the brackets are: 10% up to $12,400; 12% to $50,400; 22% to $105,700.

This filer's marginal rate is 22% (their next dollar is taxed at 22%), but their effective rate is only $7,912 ÷ $60,000 ≈ 13.2%. Earning one more dollar never lowers your total take-home — only the newest dollars sit in the top bracket.

Total tax divided by total income
blocks.explain: The effective rate is total tax paid divided by total income — the true average. The marginal rate applies only to the last dollar.

lessons.title: Deductions, credits, and tax-advantaged accounts
glossary: standard deduction
A flat amount subtracted from AGI that most filers take instead of itemizing.
itemized deduction
Adding up specific deductible expenses (mortgage interest, state taxes, charity) when they exceed the standard deduction.
tax deduction
An amount subtracted from taxable income, saving tax at your marginal rate.
tax credit
A dollar-for-dollar reduction of the tax you owe — more valuable than a deduction of the same size.
tax-advantaged account
An account (401k, IRA, HSA, 529) that reduces, defers, or eliminates tax on contributions or growth.

blocks.html: Deductions and credits both cut your bill, but not equally. A <mark>tax deduction</mark> lowers your taxable income, so it saves tax at your marginal rate. A <mark>tax credit</mark> lowers your tax bill dollar-for-dollar. A $1,000 deduction at a 22% marginal rate saves $220; a $1,000 credit saves the full $1,000.

blocks.html: Most filers take the <mark>standard deduction</mark> — a flat subtraction from AGI — because it exceeds their <mark>itemized deduction</mark> total. You itemize only when your deductible expenses (mortgage interest, state and local taxes, large charitable gifts) add up to more than the standard amount.

blocks.text: Tax-advantaged accounts are the real lever

blocks.html: The most powerful everyday tax move is using <mark>tax-advantaged accounts</mark>. Contributing to a traditional 401(k) or IRA reduces this year's taxable income. An HSA is triple tax-advantaged (deductible in, tax-free growth, tax-free medical withdrawals). A 529 grows tax-free for education. These are covered in depth in the Retirement module.

items: Withholding — tax your employer sends to the IRS from each paycheck; a large refund means you over-withheld and lent the government money interest-free.
Estimated payments — quarterly payments the self-employed make since no one withholds for them.
Tax-deferred — you pay tax later, on withdrawal (traditional accounts).
Tax-free — you pay tax now and never again on qualified growth (Roth accounts).

blocks.label: A refund is not a bonus
blocks.html: A big refund feels great but means you overpaid all year. Adjusting your W-4 withholding to break even puts that money in your paycheck — and your investments — months sooner.

blocks.q: Which saves more tax: a $1,000 deduction or a $1,000 credit (assume a 22% marginal rate)?
options: The credit, because it cuts tax dollar-for-dollar
blocks.explain: A credit reduces tax owed dollar-for-dollar ($1,000), while a deduction only saves your marginal rate on that amount ($220).

questions.q: In a progressive tax system, moving into a higher bracket means:
options: All your income is taxed at the higher rate
Only income within that bracket is taxed at the higher rate
Your effective rate equals your marginal rate
questions.explain: Only the income that falls inside the higher bracket is taxed at that rate; lower brackets keep their lower rates.

questions.q: The effective tax rate is:
options: The rate on your last dollar
Total tax divided by total income
Always higher than the marginal rate
questions.explain: Effective rate is your true average: total tax paid divided by total income.

questions.q: A tax credit differs from a deduction because a credit:
questions.explain: A credit subtracts directly from tax owed, making it more valuable than a deduction of the same dollar amount.

questions.q: Most taxpayers take the standard deduction because:
options: Their itemized deductions are smaller than it
questions.explain: You take whichever is larger; for most filers the standard deduction exceeds their itemizable expenses.

questions.q: Receiving a very large tax refund usually means you:
options: Over-withheld and lent the government money interest-free
questions.explain: A large refund means too much was withheld all year; adjusting the W-4 keeps that money in your paycheck sooner.

questions.q: The rate applied to your next dollar of income is your ______ tax rate. (one word)
questions.explain: The marginal rate is your top bracket — the rate on the next dollar earned.

questions.q: Which are tax-advantaged accounts?
questions.explain: 401(k)s, Roth IRAs, and HSAs all carry tax advantages. A standard taxable brokerage account does not.

questions.q: Adjusted gross income (AGI) is:
questions.explain: AGI is gross income minus above-the-line adjustments; the standard or itemized deduction is subtracted after AGI to get taxable income.

modules.title: Investing Fundamentals
modules.tagline: Own the whole haystack instead of searching for needles.
objectives: Distinguish saving from investing and stocks from bonds
Explain the risk-return tradeoff and why diversification reduces risk without cutting expected return
Describe why low-cost index funds are a common default and how fees compound
Choose an asset allocation based on time horizon and risk tolerance

lessons.title: Saving vs investing, stocks vs bonds
glossary: saving
Setting money aside in low-risk, liquid accounts to preserve it.
investing
Deploying money into assets with expected long-term growth, accepting short-term volatility.
stock
A share of ownership in a company; owners share in profits and growth but bear the most risk.
bond
A loan to a government or company that pays interest and returns principal at maturity; lower risk, lower return than stocks.
volatility
The degree to which an investment's price swings up and down over time.

blocks.html: <mark>Saving</mark> keeps money safe, stable, and liquid — a bank account for your emergency fund. <mark>Investing</mark> accepts short-term ups and downs in exchange for higher expected long-term growth. Both matter: your emergency fund is saved; your retirement is invested. Confusing the two — investing money you will need next month, or saving money you will not touch for 30 years — is a common, costly error.

items.label: Stocks (equities)
items.html: Ownership in companies. Highest expected long-run return, highest <mark>volatility</mark>. Historically ~10% nominal annual average for the broad U.S. market, but with steep drops along the way.

items.label: Bonds (fixed income)
items.html: Loans that pay interest. Lower expected return, much smaller swings. They cushion a portfolio when stocks fall.

items.label: Cash
items.html: Safest and most liquid, but loses purchasing power to inflation over time. For spending needs, not growth.

blocks.html: Volatility is not the same as loss. A diversified stock portfolio has fallen 30-50% in past crashes and always eventually recovered to new highs. The permanent loss comes from selling during the drop. Time horizon is what converts volatility from a threat into a non-issue.

blocks.label: Volatility is the price of admission
blocks.html: Long-term stock returns are the reward investors receive precisely because they must endure the downturns. If you want the ~7% real return, you must be able to stay invested through the scary years.

blocks.q: Money you will need for rent next month should be:
options: Saved in a liquid, stable account
Used to buy a single company's stock
blocks.explain: Short-term money must be safe and available. Investing it exposes it to volatility right when you need it.

lessons.title: Risk, return, and diversification
glossary: risk-return tradeoff
The principle that higher expected returns come only with higher risk.
diversification
Spreading money across many holdings so no single failure is catastrophic.
systematic risk
Market-wide risk that affects nearly all assets and cannot be diversified away.
unsystematic risk
Risk specific to one company or sector that diversification can largely eliminate.

blocks.html: The risk-return tradeoff is the central law of investing: no asset offers high expected returns with low risk. If someone promises both, it is a red flag. Your job is not to avoid risk but to take compensated risk and shed uncompensated risk.

That is exactly what <mark>diversification</mark> does. Owning one company exposes you to <mark>unsystematic risk</mark> — that specific firm can go to zero (Enron, Lehman). Owning thousands of companies means any single failure barely registers. Diversification is famously the only 'free lunch' in finance: it reduces risk without reducing expected return.

blocks.caption: Adding holdings kills company-specific risk; the market-risk floor remains.

blocks.html: Note the shape: most of the benefit arrives by roughly 20-30 well-chosen holdings, and a total-market index fund gives you thousands at once. You cannot diversify away <mark>systematic risk</mark> — the risk that the whole market falls — and that residual risk is precisely what earns the equity return.

Diversification is like a ship with watertight compartments. A leak in one flooded compartment is survivable; without the bulkheads, a single breach sinks the vessel. Holding one stock is a hull with no compartments.

blocks.q: Diversification is called a 'free lunch' because it:
options: Reduces risk without reducing expected return
blocks.explain: Diversification removes uncompensated company-specific risk while leaving expected return intact — a rare benefit with no offsetting cost.

lessons.title: Index funds and the tyranny of fees
glossary: index fund
A fund that holds every security in a market index at very low cost, aiming to match the market rather than beat it.
expense ratio
The annual percentage fee a fund charges, deducted from your returns.
actively managed fund
A fund where managers pick securities trying to beat the market, usually at higher cost.
passive investing
Buying and holding broad index funds rather than trading to beat the market.

blocks.html: An index fund does not try to beat the market — it is the market, holding every stock in an index like the S&P 500 in proportion. Decades of evidence show that the large majority of actively managed funds underperform their index over 10-15 years, largely because of fees and the mathematical difficulty of consistently outguessing millions of other investors.
Fees seem tiny but compound viciously. Compare two funds returning 7% before fees on $100,000 over 30 years:

A seemingly trivial 0.96% difference in expense ratio costs roughly $178,000 — about 24% of the final balance — because the fee is skimmed every year off a compounding base. This is why fee minimization is one of the few things in investing genuinely within your control.

blocks.caption: Same 7% gross return; the 0.04% index fund ends ~$178k higher than the 1% fund.

blocks.label: The one number to check
blocks.html: Before buying any fund, find its expense ratio. Broad index funds commonly charge 0.03-0.10%. If a fund charges over 0.50%, ask what you are getting for the extra cost — usually the answer is 'lower returns'.

blocks.q: An expense ratio is:
options: The annual percentage a fund charges, deducted from returns
blocks.explain: The expense ratio is an annual fee skimmed from your assets every year, which compounds into a large drag over decades.

lessons.title: Asset allocation and rebalancing
glossary: asset allocation
How a portfolio is divided among stocks, bonds, and cash — the biggest driver of long-run results.
time horizon
How long until you need the money; longer horizons can tolerate more stock risk.
risk tolerance
How much short-term loss you can accept, emotionally and financially, without selling.
rebalancing
Periodically restoring your target allocation by selling what grew and buying what lagged.
target-date fund
A single fund that holds a diversified mix and automatically grows more conservative as a target retirement year approaches.

blocks.html: Your <mark>asset allocation</mark> — the split between stocks, bonds, and cash — explains the large majority of your portfolio's risk and return, far more than which specific funds you pick. Set it from two inputs: your <mark>time horizon</mark> and your <mark>risk tolerance</mark>.
A common rough heuristic is to hold a stock percentage near 110 minus your age — a 30-year-old around 80% stocks. It is a starting point, not a rule; adjust for your real risk tolerance.

Over time, winners grow and drift your allocation away from target. A 80/20 portfolio after a stock boom might become 88/12 — riskier than you chose. <mark>Rebalancing</mark> means selling some of the winner and buying the laggard to restore 80/20. It mechanically enforces 'sell high, buy low' and controls risk. Once a year is plenty.

blocks.label: The one-fund solution
blocks.html: A <mark>target-date fund</mark> holds a globally diversified stock/bond mix and automatically rebalances and de-risks as your retirement year approaches. For many investors, a single low-cost target-date fund is a complete, hands-off portfolio.

blocks.q: Rebalancing a portfolio back to its target allocation typically involves:
options: Selling the asset that lagged and buying the winner
Selling some of the winner and buying the laggard
Adding only new money to stocks
blocks.explain: Rebalancing trims the outperformer and adds to the underperformer, restoring your risk level and enforcing sell-high, buy-low.

questions.q: The risk-return tradeoff states that:
options: High returns come with low risk
Higher expected returns require accepting higher risk
questions.explain: There is no free high return; greater expected reward always comes with greater risk.

questions.q: Diversification primarily reduces which kind of risk?
questions.explain: Diversification removes company-specific risk. Market-wide systematic risk remains and is what earns the equity return.

questions.q: An index fund's goal is to:
options: Beat the market by picking winners
Match a market index at very low cost
questions.explain: Index funds aim to match, not beat, the market, and do so cheaply — which most active funds fail to beat over the long run.

questions.q: A 0.96% higher expense ratio over 30 years matters because:
options: The fee compounds against a growing balance every year
It only affects the first year
questions.explain: An annual fee is skimmed off a compounding base each year, so small percentages become large dollar losses over decades.

questions.q: The single biggest driver of a portfolio's long-run risk and return is:
questions.explain: Asset allocation — the stock/bond/cash split — explains most of a portfolio's behavior, more than individual selection.

questions.q: Periodically restoring your target stock/bond mix by selling winners and buying laggards is called ______. (one word)
questions.explain: Rebalancing restores your chosen allocation and mechanically enforces selling high and buying low.

questions.q: Which are generally true of a longer time horizon?
options: It can tolerate more stock risk
Compounding has more time to work
questions.explain: A long horizon lets you ride out volatility and gives compounding time. Holding only cash would waste that horizon.

questions.q: A target-date fund is attractive because it:
options: Automatically diversifies, rebalances, and de-risks over time
questions.explain: A target-date fund is a hands-off, diversified portfolio that rebalances and grows more conservative as the target year nears.

modules.title: Retirement Accounts: 401(k), IRA & Roth
modules.tagline: The government hands out decades of tax-free growth — if you use the right container.
objectives: Explain tax-deferred versus tax-free growth and when each wins
Describe 401(k) mechanics, the employer match, and contribution limits
Contrast Traditional and Roth IRAs and the logic of each
Sequence contributions to maximize match, tax benefit, and flexibility

lessons.title: Tax-deferred vs tax-free: the core mechanic
glossary: tax-deferred
Contributions reduce taxable income now; you pay ordinary income tax on withdrawals in retirement (Traditional accounts).
tax-free
Contributions are made with after-tax money; qualified withdrawals, including all growth, are never taxed (Roth accounts).
employer match
Money your employer contributes to your 401(k) based on your own contributions — an immediate return.
vesting
The schedule over which employer-contributed money legally becomes yours.
contribution limit
The maximum the IRS lets you contribute to an account per year.

blocks.html: Retirement accounts are not investments themselves — they are tax-advantaged containers you put investments (like index funds) inside. The two flavors differ only in when you pay tax.

tabs.label: Traditional (tax-deferred)
tabs.html: You contribute pre-tax dollars, lowering this year's taxable income. The money grows untaxed, and you pay ordinary income tax on withdrawals in retirement. Best when your tax rate is higher now than it will be later.

tabs.label: Roth (tax-free)
tabs.html: You contribute after-tax dollars (no break today). The money grows and is withdrawn completely tax-free in retirement. Best when your tax rate is lower now than it will be later — often true for younger or lower-income earners.

blocks.html: Worked intuition. Suppose you invest $6,000 that grows 10x to $60,000. In a Roth, you already paid tax on the $6,000 and owe nothing on the $60,000. In a Traditional account you deducted the $6,000 up front but owe ordinary income tax on the full $60,000 at withdrawal. Roth shelters the growth from tax entirely — which is why it is so powerful when growth is large.

blocks.label: Limits and figures change yearly
blocks.html: Contribution limits are indexed to inflation. For 2026: 401(k) employee limit is $24,500; IRA limit is $7,500; those 50+ get catch-up contributions. Always confirm the current year's limits with the IRS.

blocks.q: In a Roth account, the investment growth at qualified withdrawal is:
blocks.explain: Roth contributions are made with after-tax money, so all qualified withdrawals — including decades of growth — come out completely tax-free.

lessons.title: The 401(k) and the free-money match
glossary: An employer-sponsored retirement plan funded by payroll deductions, often with an employer match.
Roth 401(k)
A 401(k) option funded with after-tax dollars for tax-free qualified withdrawals.
automatic enrollment
A plan feature that starts new employees contributing by default unless they opt out.

blocks.html: A <mark>401(k)</mark> is an employer-sponsored account funded straight from your paycheck before you ever see the money — which makes it powerfully automatic. Many employers offer a <mark>match</mark>: they contribute alongside you, up to a limit.

The match is the highest-return move in personal finance. A common formula is '100% match on the first 3%, then 50% on the next 2%.' If you earn $60,000 and contribute 5% ($3,000), the employer adds $2,400 — an instant, guaranteed 80% return on that contribution, before any market growth.

blocks.title: How a 4% full match works on $60,000 salary

blocks.label: Never leave the match on the table
blocks.html: Failing to contribute enough to capture the full match is turning down a raise. Before paying down anything but the highest-interest debt, contribute at least enough to get every matched dollar. Watch <mark>vesting</mark> — matched money may only become fully yours after a few years of service.

Many plans offer a <mark>Roth 401(k)</mark> option, combining the high 401(k) contribution limit and match with Roth tax-free growth. Note: the employer's matching dollars always go into a traditional (pre-tax) bucket even if your own contributions are Roth.

blocks.q: An employer offers a 100% match on the first 4% of salary. You earn $50,000 and contribute 4%. How much 'free' money does the employer add?
blocks.explain: 4% of $50,000 is $2,000, and a 100% match adds an equal $2,000 — an instant doubling of that contribution.

lessons.title: IRAs and the contribution priority ladder
glossary: IRA
Individual Retirement Account — a tax-advantaged account you open yourself, independent of an employer.
Traditional IRA
An IRA with potentially tax-deductible contributions and tax-deferred growth.
Roth IRA
An IRA funded with after-tax dollars offering tax-free qualified growth and flexible contribution withdrawals.
income phase-out
Income thresholds above which the ability to contribute to or deduct an account is reduced or eliminated.

blocks.html: An IRA is a retirement account you open yourself at a brokerage, separate from any employer. It comes in Traditional and Roth versions with the same tax logic as the 401(k). The Roth IRA is especially prized for one feature: because you already paid tax on contributions, you can withdraw your contributions (not earnings) at any time, penalty-free — a rare bit of flexibility.

blocks.label: Roth IRAs have income limits
blocks.html: High earners face an <mark>income phase-out</mark> that reduces or blocks direct Roth IRA contributions. 401(k)s have no such income limit, which is one reason to max the workplace plan too.

items: 401(k) up to the full employer match — capture every free dollar first; nothing else returns 50-100% instantly.
Pay off high-interest debt — a guaranteed return equal to the APR (see the Debt module).
Fund an emergency fund — so a surprise never forces you to raid retirement accounts.
Max a Roth or Traditional IRA — broad investment choice and, for Roth, tax-free growth and flexibility.
Return to the 401(k) and contribute toward the annual limit.
Taxable brokerage account — unlimited, flexible, for anything beyond the tax-advantaged limits.

blocks.q: Why does the priority ladder put 'contribute to the 401(k) match' before 'max out an IRA'?
options: The match is an immediate guaranteed 50-100% return unavailable anywhere else
blocks.explain: The employer match is an instant, guaranteed return that no other step can offer, so it comes first.

questions.q: A Traditional 401(k) contribution:
options: Reduces your taxable income now and is taxed on withdrawal
questions.explain: Traditional contributions are pre-tax (deductible now) and taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn in retirement.

questions.q: The defining benefit of a Roth account is that:
options: Qualified withdrawals, including growth, are tax-free
questions.explain: Roth accounts use after-tax contributions so all qualified withdrawals, including decades of growth, are tax-free.

questions.q: An employer match should be captured before most other goals because it is:
questions.explain: The match is free money — an instant, guaranteed return no investment can match — so it comes first.

questions.q: A Roth is generally most advantageous when your tax rate is:
options: Higher now than it will be in retirement
Lower now than it will be in retirement
questions.explain: Paying tax now (Roth) wins when your current rate is lower than your expected future rate, common for younger earners.

questions.q: A distinctive flexibility of the Roth IRA is that you can withdraw your ______ at any time penalty-free.
questions.explain: Because contributions were already taxed, your contributions (not earnings) can be withdrawn anytime without penalty.

questions.q: Money your employer adds to your 401(k) based on your own contributions is called the employer ______. (one word)
questions.explain: The employer match is an immediate guaranteed return and the first priority in most contribution ladders.

questions.q: Which statements about retirement accounts are true?
options: They are containers that hold investments
Roth withdrawals of qualified growth are tax-free
questions.explain: Accounts are tax-advantaged containers; 401(k)s are employer plans; Roth growth is tax-free. IRAs are opened by individuals, no employer needed.

questions.q: The employer's matching dollars in a Roth 401(k) are:
options: Also placed in the Roth (after-tax) bucket
questions.explain: Even when your own contributions are Roth, the employer's match goes into a traditional pre-tax bucket.

modules.title: Insurance & Risk Management
modules.tagline: Insurance is not an investment — it is how you keep one setback from erasing a decade.
objectives: Explain how insurance transfers catastrophic risk and why to self-insure small risks
Reason about premiums, deductibles, and the deductible-premium tradeoff
Identify the core policies most adults need and match coverage to actual risk
Distinguish term from permanent life insurance and size a life policy

lessons.title: The logic of insurance
glossary: insurance
A contract that transfers the financial risk of a large, unlikely loss to an insurer in exchange for a premium.
premium
The recurring amount you pay to keep an insurance policy active.
deductible
The amount you pay out of pocket before insurance begins to cover a claim.
self-insure
Choosing to bear a small potential loss yourself rather than pay to insure it.
risk transfer
Shifting the financial consequences of a risk from yourself to another party, such as an insurer.

blocks.html: Insurance exists to transfer catastrophic risk — the low-probability, high-cost events that could bankrupt you. You pay a small, predictable premium so the insurer absorbs a rare, enormous loss. The correct mental model: insure what you cannot afford to replace; self-insure what you can.

head: Risk
Insure or self-insure?
Why
rows: Catastrophic; you cannot absorb a $400,000 loss
Small and affordable; premiums exceed expected cost
Bills can reach six figures fast
Replacement is cheap; the warranty is pure profit for the seller

blocks.html: This is why extended warranties, phone insurance, and low deductibles are often poor deals: they insure losses you could comfortably pay yourself, and the premium must cover the seller's profit and overhead. Insurance is priced to lose you a little money on average — you buy it only when the tail risk is unbearable.

Insurance is a fire escape, not a gym membership. You are not trying to 'get your money's worth' by using it — a good year is one where you paid the premium and never filed a claim. Its value is protection from the year that would otherwise ruin you.

blocks.q: According to the insure/self-insure principle, you should buy insurance for:
options: Large, unlikely losses you could not absorb
blocks.explain: Insurance is for catastrophic losses you cannot afford. Small losses are cheaper to self-insure than to pay premiums on.

lessons.title: Premiums, deductibles, and the coverage you need
glossary: out-of-pocket maximum
The most you will pay in a year for covered health care before insurance pays 100%.
term life insurance
Pure, low-cost life coverage for a fixed period (e.g., 20 years) with no investment component.
permanent life insurance
Life coverage that lasts for life and includes a cash-value component, at much higher cost.
liability coverage
Insurance that pays for harm you cause to others, protecting your assets from lawsuits.
disability insurance
Insurance that replaces part of your income if illness or injury stops you from working.

blocks.html: There is a direct tradeoff between the <mark>deductible</mark> and the <mark>premium</mark>: choosing a higher deductible lowers your premium, because you agree to absorb more of any loss yourself. If you have a solid emergency fund, a higher deductible usually wins on average — you self-insure the routine and pay less every month.

blocks.text: The core policies most adults need

items.label: Health insurance
items.html: Non-negotiable — a serious illness is the fastest route to bankruptcy. Watch the <mark>out-of-pocket maximum</mark>, your true worst case.

items.label: Auto / renters / homeowners
items.html: Property plus <mark>liability coverage</mark>, which protects your assets if you injure someone or damage property.

items.label: Disability insurance
items.html: Your income is your biggest asset. <mark>Disability insurance</mark> replaces part of it if you cannot work — statistically more likely than dying young.

items.label: Term life insurance
items.html: Essential if others depend on your income (partner, children). Cheap and simple.

blocks.html: Term vs permanent life. Term life insurance is pure protection: cheap coverage for a set period, chosen to cover the years your dependents need your income. Permanent life insurance bundles insurance with a costly investment component and is far more expensive per dollar of coverage. For most people, the guidance is 'buy term and invest the difference' — keep insurance and investing in separate, low-cost containers.
A common rule of thumb sizes term life coverage at roughly 10-12x your annual income, adjusted for debts (like a mortgage) and dependents' future needs (like college).

blocks.label: If no one depends on your income
blocks.html: A single person with no dependents and no co-signed debt usually needs little or no life insurance. Do not let a salesperson sell protection for a risk you do not carry.

blocks.q: Choosing a higher deductible on a policy generally results in:
options: A lower premium because you absorb more of any loss
blocks.explain: A higher deductible shifts more of the risk to you, so the insurer charges a lower premium in exchange.

questions.q: The primary purpose of insurance is to:
options: Transfer catastrophic, unaffordable risk to an insurer
questions.explain: Insurance transfers rare, large losses you could not absorb; small losses are better self-insured.

questions.q: Extended warranties on cheap items are usually poor deals because:
options: They insure affordable losses and must cover the seller's profit
questions.explain: You are paying to insure a loss you could easily cover yourself, plus the seller's margin — so on average you lose.

questions.q: Raising your deductible typically:
questions.explain: A higher deductible means you shoulder more of any loss, so the insurer lowers your premium.

questions.q: For most people supporting dependents, the recommended life insurance is:
options: Low-cost term life, investing the difference separately
questions.explain: 'Buy term and invest the difference' keeps cheap protection and low-cost investing in separate containers.

questions.q: Disability insurance matters because:
options: Your income is your biggest asset and disability is more likely than early death
questions.explain: Losing the ability to work destroys your income stream, and disability during working years is statistically more likely than dying young.

questions.q: The amount you pay out of pocket before insurance begins covering a claim is the ______. (one word)
questions.explain: The deductible is your share before coverage kicks in; higher deductibles lower premiums.

questions.q: Which policies do most working adults with dependents need?
questions.explain: Health, term life, and disability cover catastrophic risks. A toaster warranty insures a trivial, affordable loss.

questions.q: A single person with no dependents and no co-signed debt generally needs:
questions.explain: Life insurance replaces income others depend on; with no dependents, there is little to insure.

modules.title: Behavioral Finance
modules.tagline: The biggest threat to your portfolio is usually the person holding it.
objectives: Identify common cognitive biases that sabotage financial decisions
Explain the behavior gap between fund returns and investor returns
Use precommitment, automation, and rules to defend against your own impulses
Recognize lifestyle inflation and loss aversion in your own behavior

lessons.title: The biases that cost you money
glossary: loss aversion
The tendency to feel losses about twice as intensely as equivalent gains, driving panic selling.
recency bias
Overweighting recent events, expecting the recent past to continue indefinitely.
herd behavior
Following the crowd into or out of investments, often buying high and selling low.
present bias
Overvaluing immediate rewards over larger future ones, undermining saving.
mental accounting
Treating money differently based on arbitrary labels (a 'bonus' vs 'salary') rather than as fungible.

blocks.html: Classical economics assumes people are rational. Decades of research in behavioral finance show we are predictably irrational — and those predictable errors have price tags. Knowing the biases by name is the first step to catching yourself in the act.

cards.label: Loss aversion
cards.html: <mark>Loss aversion</mark>: losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good. This drives investors to panic-sell during crashes — locking in the loss they most fear.

cards.label: Recency bias
cards.html: <mark>Recency bias</mark>: assuming the recent trend continues. It makes people pile into what just went up and flee what just went down — the opposite of buy-low, sell-high.

cards.label: Herd behavior
cards.html: <mark>Herd behavior</mark>: comfort in the crowd. Bubbles and panics are herd behavior at scale; the crowd is most confident at the top and most fearful at the bottom.

cards.label: Present bias
cards.html: <mark>Present bias</mark>: valuing $100 today far above $110 next year. It is why saving for a distant retirement feels so hard and instant purchases feel so easy.

cards.label: Mental accounting
cards.html: <mark>Mental accounting</mark>: treating a tax refund as 'fun money' while carrying 22% credit-card debt. Money is fungible; a dollar is a dollar regardless of its label.

blocks.label: The most dangerous phrase
blocks.html: 'This time is different' has preceded nearly every bubble and crash. Recency bias and herd behavior together convince smart people to abandon their plan at exactly the wrong moment.

blocks.q: An investor sells everything after a 30% market drop, locking in the loss. Which bias is most at work?
blocks.explain: Loss aversion makes the pain of the paper loss unbearable, driving the panic sale that converts a temporary decline into a permanent loss.

lessons.title: The behavior gap and how to beat it
glossary: behavior gap
The shortfall between the return an investment earned and the lower return its average investor actually captured, caused by poorly timed buying and selling.
lifestyle inflation
The tendency for spending to rise to match rising income, so higher pay does not raise the savings rate.
precommitment
Binding your future self to a plan in advance, before emotion or temptation arrives.
dollar-cost averaging
Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule regardless of price, removing timing decisions.

blocks.html: Here is the punchline of behavioral finance: the average investor earns meaningfully less than the funds they invest in. Studies repeatedly find a behavior gap of a percentage point or more per year — the fund returns 7%, but the average holder captures 5-6% because they bought after rallies and sold during crashes. The gap is self-inflicted, and it compounds.

blocks.html: You cannot delete your biases, but you can <mark>precommit</mark> around them — bind your rational self today so your emotional self cannot override the plan tomorrow.

items: Automate everything. Auto-transfer to savings and auto-invest on payday. A decision you make once cannot be sabotaged by a bad mood — this is dollar-cost averaging in practice.
Write an investment policy statement. One page: your allocation, contribution rate, and a pledge not to sell during downturns. Read it when markets scare you.
Check your portfolio less. Daily checking amplifies loss aversion; a long-term investor gains nothing from watching the noise.
Bank your raises. When income rises, automatically route part of the increase to savings before it becomes spending — this defeats lifestyle inflation.
Impose a waiting period. A 48-hour rule on large discretionary purchases neutralizes present bias and impulse.

blocks.label: Boring is a strategy
blocks.html: The optimal investor behavior is almost aggressively dull: pick a low-cost diversified allocation, automate contributions, rebalance once a year, and otherwise do nothing. The urge to 'do something' during volatility is the enemy, not a signal.

blocks.q: Automating your investments on payday primarily defends against which problem?
options: The behavior gap from emotional, poorly timed buying and selling
blocks.explain: Automation removes the emotional timing decisions that create the behavior gap, so you invest steadily regardless of mood or headlines.

questions.q: Loss aversion describes the tendency to:
options: Feel losses roughly twice as intensely as equal gains
questions.explain: Losses hurt about twice as much as equivalent gains feel good, which drives panic selling in downturns.

questions.q: The behavior gap refers to:
options: The shortfall between fund returns and what the average investor actually earns
The gap between stocks and bonds
questions.explain: Poorly timed buying and selling causes the average investor to capture less than the fund itself returned.

questions.q: Automating investments on payday helps mainly by:
questions.explain: Automation enforces steady investing regardless of emotion, closing the behavior gap.

questions.q: Lifestyle inflation is best countered by:
options: Automatically saving part of each raise before it becomes spending
questions.explain: Routing part of every raise to savings before you adjust to the higher income keeps your savings rate rising.

questions.q: 'This time is different' is dangerous because it reflects:
options: Recency bias and herd behavior at market extremes
questions.explain: The phrase captures recency bias and herding, which have preceded most bubbles and crashes.

questions.q: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule regardless of price is called dollar-cost ______. (one word)
questions.explain: Dollar-cost averaging removes timing decisions and is naturally implemented by automating contributions.

questions.q: Which are effective defenses against your own biases?
options: Imposing a waiting period on big purchases
questions.explain: Automation, a written policy, and waiting periods precommit your rational self. Frequent checking amplifies loss aversion.

questions.q: Treating a tax refund as 'fun money' while carrying high-interest debt is an example of:
questions.explain: Mental accounting labels fungible money differently; rationally, that refund should attack the 22% debt first.

modules.title: Capstone: Build Your Personal Financial Plan
modules.tagline: Turn every module into one page you will actually follow.
objectives: Synthesize budgeting, debt, savings, and investing into a single coherent plan
Compute your own savings rate, emergency-fund target, and debt-payoff timeline
Choose an asset allocation and account priority consistent with your goals
Produce a written, automatable one-page financial plan

lessons.title: Assembling the plan
glossary: net worth
Total assets minus total liabilities; the single best snapshot of overall financial health.
financial goal
A specific, dated, dollar-quantified target such as 'a $15,000 emergency fund within 18 months'.
automation
Setting up transfers and investments to run without ongoing decisions, protecting the plan from willpower and emotion.

blocks.html: A financial plan is not a spreadsheet you admire once — it is a short set of decisions, made calmly in advance, that you then <mark>automate</mark> and mostly ignore. This capstone walks you through building yours from the pieces of every prior module.

blocks.title: The seven-step build
steps: Compute your <mark>net worth</mark> (assets minus liabilities) and your current monthly cash flow.
Assign every take-home dollar to needs, wants, and savings; compute your savings rate.
Set a target of 3-6 months of essential expenses and a monthly amount to reach it.
List every debt with its APR; pick avalanche or snowball and compute a payoff date.
Capture the full match, choose an account priority, and set an asset allocation.
Confirm health, liability, disability, and (if dependents) term life coverage.
Schedule automatic transfers and one calendar reminder per year to rebalance and revisit.

blocks.html: Set <mark>financial goals</mark> that are specific and dated — 'save $15,000 for an emergency fund within 18 months' beats 'save more.' A dated dollar target converts directly into a required monthly transfer you can automate: $15,000 ÷ 18 ≈ $834/month.

blocks.label: The plan fits on one page
blocks.html: If your plan does not fit on a single page, it is too complicated to follow. Complexity is not sophistication; a boring, automated, one-page plan beats an elaborate one you abandon in March.

blocks.q: Why convert a financial goal into a specific dated dollar amount?
options: Because it translates directly into a monthly transfer you can automate
Because vague goals earn higher returns
blocks.explain: A dated dollar target divides cleanly into a required monthly amount, which you can then automate — turning intention into action.

lessons.title: The capstone assignment
glossary: investment policy statement
A brief written document stating your allocation, contribution rate, and rules, used to resist emotional decisions.

blocks.html: Now build the real thing for your own situation (or a realistic hypothetical). Use actual or plausible numbers so the arithmetic is concrete. The rubric below defines what a strong submission demonstrates — treat each item as a checkbox your plan must satisfy.

blocks.title: Assignment: Your one-page personal financial plan
blocks.brief: Produce a single-page written plan for a real or realistic household. Show your numbers and the reasoning behind each choice, drawing on every module. Include a short investment policy statement and a disclaimer that this is your own educational plan, not professional advice.
items: A monthly budget that assigns every take-home dollar to needs, wants, and savings, with a computed savings rate stated as a percentage.
A cash-flow statement showing income minus expenses and the resulting net cash flow, with any leaks identified.
An emergency-fund target sized in months of essential expenses, with the dollar figure and a dated monthly plan to reach it.
A complete debt inventory listing each balance and APR, a chosen payoff strategy (avalanche or snowball) with justification, and an estimated payoff date computed from real numbers.
A stated savings rate with a specific plan to raise it over time (e.g., banking future raises to fight lifestyle inflation).
An explicit asset allocation (stock/bond split) justified by time horizon and risk tolerance, plus a rebalancing rule.
An account-priority ladder that captures the full employer match first and sequences debt, emergency fund, IRA, and 401(k) deliberately.
An insurance checklist confirming health, liability, disability, and (if applicable) term life coverage, with any gaps named.
A one-paragraph investment policy statement pledging to automate contributions and not sell during downturns.
Evidence of automation: which transfers run automatically, on what dates, and one annual review date on the calendar.
A clear education-not-advice disclaimer and correct, current figures where limits or brackets are cited.

blocks.label: A plan you will not follow is worthless
blocks.html: The best plan is not the mathematically optimal one — it is the one you will actually execute for years. Favor simplicity, automation, and rules you can keep when markets and moods turn against you.

Keep your <mark>investment policy statement</mark> somewhere you will see it during the next market panic. It is a letter from your calm self to your frightened future self, and rereading it is often the difference between staying invested and joining the behavior gap.

blocks.q: What is the single most important quality of a good personal financial plan?
options: It uses the most sophisticated math
It is one you will actually follow and automate for years
It beats the market every year
blocks.explain: A simple, automated plan you sustain for years beats an optimal one you abandon. Execution over elegance.

questions.q: Net worth is calculated as:
questions.explain: Net worth is assets minus liabilities — the clearest snapshot of overall financial health.

questions.q: A strong financial goal is:
options: 'Save $15,000 for an emergency fund within 18 months'
questions.explain: Specific, dated, dollar-quantified goals convert directly into an automatable monthly amount.

questions.q: In the account-priority ladder, the first dollar should go to:
questions.explain: The employer match is an instant guaranteed return, so it is the first priority in the ladder.

questions.q: The most important quality of a financial plan is that it:
options: Is one you will actually follow and automate
questions.explain: Sustainable execution beats theoretical optimality; a plan abandoned in March helps no one.

questions.q: An investment policy statement is useful mainly because it:
options: Helps you resist emotional selling during downturns
questions.explain: It records your rules in advance so your frightened future self does not override the plan and widen the behavior gap.

questions.q: Setting transfers and investments to run without ongoing decisions is called ______. (one word)
questions.explain: Automation protects the plan from willpower and emotion by removing repeated decisions.

questions.q: A strong one-page plan should include which of the following?
options: A savings rate and emergency-fund target
A debt inventory with APRs and a payoff strategy
An asset allocation with a rebalancing rule
A promise to time the market
questions.explain: Savings rate, debt plan, and allocation are core. Market timing is precisely what the plan is designed to avoid.

questions.q: Banking your future raises is a plan feature that specifically counters:
questions.explain: Routing raises to savings before they become spending prevents lifestyle inflation from eating higher income.

resources.title: Go deeper
items: "I Will Teach You to Be Rich" — Ramit Sethi
A practical, automation-first system for budgeting and paying yourself first.

Short essays on behavior, why temperament beats intelligence in investing.

The clearest popular case for low-cost, total-market index investing.

The academic foundation for passive investing and market efficiency.

Free, unbiased government worksheets and plain-language guides on budgeting, debt, and credit.

The authoritative source for current tax brackets, deductions, and retirement-account contribution limits.
Bogleheads.org wiki
A respected community reference on sensible, low-cost, long-term investing.

questions.q: The foundational habit behind any working budget is:
questions.explain: You cannot manage what you do not measure; tracking reveals reality before you set targets.

questions.q: A monthly budget should be built on:
questions.explain: Take-home pay is the money you actually control after taxes and deductions.

questions.q: An emergency fund should be sized on:
questions.explain: The fund covers essentials during a disruption, so it is measured in months of essential expenses.

questions.q: $10,000 invested at 7% compounded annually for 30 years grows to approximately:
questions.explain: FV = 10000 x (1.07)^30 approx $76,000; most of the gain is interest on interest.

questions.q: Using the Rule of 72, money doubles at a 6% return in about:
If investments return 7% and inflation is 3%, the real return is roughly:
questions.explain: Real return is approximately nominal minus inflation: 7% - 3% = 4%.

questions.q: In an amortizing loan, the earliest payments are mostly:
questions.explain: Interest is charged on the balance, which is largest at the start.

questions.q: The debt avalanche method targets the debt with the:
questions.explain: Attacking the highest APR first minimizes total interest paid.

questions.q: The two largest factors in a FICO credit score are:
questions.explain: Payment history (~35%) and amounts owed/utilization (~30%) dominate the score.

questions.q: The difference between marginal and effective tax rates is that the effective rate is:
options: The rate on your last dollar
Total tax divided by total income
questions.explain: Marginal is the rate on the next dollar; effective is total tax divided by total income.

questions.q: A $1,000 tax credit versus a $1,000 deduction (22% marginal rate): the credit saves:
questions.explain: A credit cuts tax dollar-for-dollar ($1,000); a deduction saves only the marginal rate ($220).

questions.q: Diversification primarily reduces:
questions.explain: Diversification removes company-specific risk; market risk remains and earns the equity return.

questions.q: A fund's expense ratio is:
options: The annual percentage skimmed from returns
questions.explain: The expense ratio is an annual fee that compounds into a large drag over decades.

questions.q: The biggest driver of a portfolio's long-run risk and return is:
questions.explain: The stock/bond/cash split explains most of a portfolio's behavior.

questions.q: An employer 401(k) match should usually be captured before other goals because it is:
questions.explain: The match is instant free money no investment can rival, so it comes first.

questions.q: The defining feature of a Roth account is that qualified withdrawals, including growth, are:
questions.explain: Roth contributions are after-tax, so qualified withdrawals, including all growth, are tax-free.

questions.q: Insurance is best used to cover:
options: Large, unlikely losses you could not absorb
questions.explain: Insurance transfers catastrophic risk; small losses are cheaper to self-insure.

questions.q: Raising a policy's deductible generally:
questions.explain: A higher deductible shifts more risk to you, so the insurer lowers the premium.

questions.q: The behavior gap is caused by:
options: Emotional, poorly timed buying and selling
questions.explain: Buying after rallies and selling in crashes makes investors capture less than the fund returned.

questions.q: Automating investments on payday mainly defends against:
options: The behavior gap from emotional timing
questions.explain: Automation removes the emotional timing decisions that create the behavior gap.

questions.q: Loss aversion means people tend to:
options: Feel losses about twice as intensely as equal gains
questions.explain: The outsized pain of loss drives panic selling during downturns.

questions.q: When investment returns themselves earn further returns over time, it is called ______. (one word)
questions.explain: Compounding — growth on prior growth — is the engine of long-term wealth.

questions.q: Periodically restoring your target stock/bond mix by selling winners and buying laggards is called ______. (one word)
questions.explain: Rebalancing restores your chosen risk level and enforces buy-low, sell-high.

questions.q: Which are sensible early priorities in a personal-finance plan?
questions.explain: The match, high-interest debt payoff, and an emergency fund are foundational. Market timing is to be avoided.

questions.q: Which habits generally help a credit score?
options: Applying for many cards at once
questions.explain: On-time payments and low utilization help; closing old cards and rapid applications hurt.
